analysis.one_liner: Caps allergy-shot insurance copays for epinephrine injectors at $60 per two-pack.
analysis.headline: The bill would cap insurance cost-sharing for epinephrine auto-injectors at $60 per two-pack with no deductible, but since its September 4, 2025 introduction it has sat in three House committees with only 2 supporters.
analysis.plain_summary: The EPIPEN Act would force group health plans and health insurers to cover FDA-approved epinephrine delivery systems — auto-injectors, nasal sprays, and sublingual products used to treat severe allergic reactions. Plans could not apply a deductible to these products and could not charge more than $60 per package of two. Cost-sharing payments would count toward deductibles and out-of-pocket maximums, and the rules would take effect for plan years starting January 1, 2026.
analysis.who_benefits: People with severe allergies who need epinephrine on hand — especially families whose plans currently apply full deductibles to auto-injectors, which can push the cost of a two-pack to several hundred dollars. They would pay at most $60 per package (or less if their plan already charges that), and every dollar paid would count toward their deductible or out-of-pocket maximum [S2]. People with high-deductible plans gain the most, since today the entire price of an injector often falls on them before coverage kicks in [S2].
analysis.who_benefits_short: People with severe allergies, especially high-deductible-plan families

how_it_helps.text: Bans deductibles on epinephrine delivery systems entirely, so a person who needs an auto-injector does not have to pay full freight at the start of a plan year — the moment they are most likely to be exposed to a fresh allergy season with an empty deductible.

Caps cost-sharing at $60 per package of two delivery systems (or the equivalent) for auto-injectors, nasal sprays, and sublingual products approved by the FDA, covering all forms of emergency epinephrine, not just one brand.
Counts the capped copay toward deductibles and out-of-pocket maximums, so people with serious conditions are not charged outside protections they are working toward.

Requires coverage under employer plans, individual and group insurance, and self-insured employer plans alike by amending the three federal laws that govern each type of coverage, with the changes effective for plan years starting on or after January 1, 2026.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and employer plans that fund coverage would absorb the difference between what patients pay (up to $60 per two-pack) and the drug's price. Plans that currently push the full cost of epinephrine onto patients through deductibles would see more claims, and those costs flow back into premiums shared by all enrollees. Epinephrine makers would face plans steering toward the cheapest products to control costs.
analysis.who_pays_short: Health insurers and employer health plans

drawbacks.text: The mandate raises costs for insurers and employer plans, and those costs do not disappear — they are recovered through premiums and employer contributions spread across all enrollees, including people who never need epinephrine.

The bill lets plans apply higher cost-sharing — or no coverage at all — when an epinephrine product comes from an out-of-network provider, so a patient who gets an injector from a pharmacy outside their plan's network gets no protection from the $60 cap.

A flat $60 cap is not adjusted for cheaper generic products; for people whose plan already covers a low-cost generic with modest copays, the bill changes little, while the mandate applies to every plan in the country regardless of how it currently handles epinephrine.

It addresses the patient's out-of-pocket cost but does nothing about the underlying list prices of epinephrine products, so the payment still flows to drug makers — the bill caps what insurers can pass through, not what manufacturers can charge.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the people who carry epinephrine, the benefit is concrete and immediate: no deductible and a hard $60 cap per two-pack, across every type of health coverage, starting in 2026. The costs are real but diffuse — higher claims for insurers and employers, recovered through modestly higher premiums across all enrollees — and the out-of-network carve-out plus the lack of any price control on manufacturers blunt the bill's reach. On balance the design is sound: it targets a narrow, medically necessary product, protects patients during the deductible phase, and applies to all forms of approved epinephrine rather than one brand.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on September 4, 2025 and referred to three House committees, where no committee has taken it up yet.

narrative.text: Rep. Maxwell Frost (D-FL) introduced the bill on September 4, 2025, joined by Rep. Doris Matsui (D-CA) as its only cosponsor.

The same day, the Speaker's office referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee, and additionally to the Education and Workforce and Ways and Means Committees, with each committee to consider the portions under its jurisdiction — a three-committee referral that means the bill must satisfy multiple chairmen to move.
In the roughly two months since referral, no committee has held a markup, reported the bill, or scheduled floor action, and the bill's only actions on record remain its introduction and referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has won or lost — the bill simply has not moved. The status quo benefits health insurers and employer plans, which continue to apply deductibles to epinephrine with no federal cap in place.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Nobody yet; insurers keep the status quo

for.name: Doris Matsui
for.role: U.S. Representative (D-CA); the bill's only cosponsor

sides.party_line_note: No one has opposed the bill on the record, but its two supporters are both Democrats, no Republican has joined, and no committee chaired by the Republican majority has acted on it.

industries.industry: Health insurers and employer health plans
industries.note: They would have to cover epinephrine for all enrollees with no deductible and a $60 cap per two-pack, absorbing the gap between the cap and the drug's price — a cost recovered through premiums. Today, high-deductible plans can push the full price of an auto-injector onto the patient.

The bill guarantees a covered market for every FDA-approved epinephrine product — auto-injectors, nasal sprays, sublingual — which locks in demand. But it caps what patients can be charged, giving insurers a strong incentive to stock the cheapest generic, so makers of premium-priced brands could lose ground.

analysis.trajectory: This bill fits a familiar pattern: a first-term member's single-issue health bill with one cosponsor, referred to three committees, with no action since. Most bills at this stage die quietly when the Congress ends. It could advance only if its provisions are folded into a larger insurance-coverage package that committee leaders choose to move; on its own, it is very unlikely to get a hearing or a vote.
